items.article: The aviation security expert said that there is no universal background check system for pilots The alleged hijacking of an Israel-bound flight has raised questions over how secure the vetting process is for one of aviation's most skilled jobs. Flydubai FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv rapidly descended during a terrifying ordeal as the co-pilot allegedly tried to take control of the plane after attacking his fellow pilot with an axe, or possibly stabbing him. It is still unclear why the co-pilot to acted in this way. Yet the question remains: how was this person able to bypass rigorous background checks and be given the responsibility of flying planes? "It's very easy after every incident to say, what more can we do?" Phillip Baum, visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, said. "Often, airline pilots are recruited from other states, so the degree of background checks is somewhat limited. They'll certainly have their pilot training and licenses, but in terms of background checks from other states, it's always a problem." Mr Baum, who has 35 years' experience in aviation security, explained that varying pilot-vetting models across countries have long created issues for the aviation industry. items.article: Kevin’s ultramarathon challenge ends in time for kick-off at Old Trafford as son Jack vies for first title with Wakefield There are few families with more stories to tell when it comes to the Super League Grand Final than the Sinfields but, even by their lofty standards, this week will take some beating. Leeds has been the epicentre of that story for more than 20 years but this week the focus has moved 10 miles down the road to Wakefield. Jack will fulfil a childhood dream by playing at Old Trafford for the first time on Saturday, when Wakefield Trinity attempt to win their maiden Super League title. Unsurprisingly his father, Kevin, will be there – but in circumstances that make this story all the more remarkable. Sinfield Sr is in the midst of his seventh and final fundraising challenge to support those living with motor neurone disease, which will conclude at Old Trafford on Saturday and passed through Wakefield on Wednesday. He will finish the last leg of his seventh ultramarathon in seven days at the Grand Final and will carry the match ball into the stadium for Wakefield’s showdown with Warrington Wolves. Waiting for him on the pitch will be his son, who first attended the event shortly after he was born, when Kevin played in the 2004 final for Leeds Rhinos . items.article: Strictly Come Dancing has been flooded with complaints since it returned last month. It was always going to be difficult for Strictly Come Dancing when it returned this year. After all, Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman fronted the show together for 11 years, and their partnership became part of the furniture. It was obvious that change was always going to be difficult. Emma Willis , Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe made their debuts last month, and unfortunately, the backlash came almost immediately. Emma, in particular, seems to have won viewers over. That makes the most sense to me, as she is the only presenter in the traditional sense. Unfortunately for Josh and Johannes, they have faced a very different reaction, with both attracting their fair share of criticism . But it's not only the main show that has come under fire. Its spin-off, It Takes Two, has also found itself at the centre of complaints from viewers . While Ellie Taylor has been praised for bringing a fresh energy to the programme, the format itself has been altered in ways that haven't gone down quite so well, with some even admitting that they're no longer watching at all. While it's clear Strictly needs to evolve, there are certain aspects that simply don't need changing. However, that doesn't apply to everything. You agree you are 18 or over.
